title: Lancashire Hotpot
subtitle: Slow-braised lamb with a golden layered potato top
excerpt: Lancashire hotpot is a slow-cooked braise of lamb neck and onions under overlapping slices of potato, baked for two hours until the potato top is golden and the lamb underneath has fallen from the bone. It is one of the great dishes of northern England: simple, filling, and better the next day.
sourceNotes: Lancashire hotpot is the defining dish of the county. Historical recipes from the nineteenth century use neck of mutton, onion, and oysters under sliced potato. The oysters were eventually dropped as the price of seafood rose, but the potato-topped braise survives as an emblem of northern English cooking.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze after baking and cooling. Defrost overnight and reheat covered at 160°C fan for 45 minutes, then uncover for 15 minutes to re-crisp the top.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make and bake the day before. Reheat as above. The flavour improves overnight.

content.text: Lancashire hotpot asks almost nothing of the cook. Lamb neck goes in with onions, thyme, and stock; sliced potato covers the top; the lid goes on for the first hour, then comes off for the second. The potato browns and crisps as the lamb underneath becomes tender and the stock reduces to a rich gravy. It is one of the most self-sufficient dishes in British cooking.

items.prepNote: bone-in neck chops or neck fillet, cut into portions
waxy or all-rounder variety, peeled and thinly sliced, about 3 mm

content.text: Heat a large casserole or Dutch oven over medium-high heat with a little oil. Brown the lamb neck pieces in batches until coloured on all sides. Set aside. In the same pot, cook {{onion}} sliced onion for 5 minutes until softened.

Return the lamb to the pot. Add {{carrot}} sliced carrots, the thyme, the bay leaves, {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce, and {{stock-beef}} of stock. Season well. The stock should come about halfway up the lamb, not cover it.
Arrange {{potato}} of thinly sliced potato overlapping in neat layers on top, covering the meat completely. Brush with {{unsalted-butter}} of melted butter. Season with salt and pepper.

Cover tightly with a lid or foil and bake at 160°C fan for 1 hour. Remove the lid and bake for a further 1 hour until the potato top is golden and the lamb is very tender when pressed with a spoon. Rest for 10 minutes before serving.

items.symptom: The potato top is pale after 2 hours
items.cause: The oven was too cool or the lid stayed on too long.
items.fix: Increase the temperature to 180°C fan for the final 20 minutes. The top needs direct dry heat to colour.

items.symptom: The lamb is still tough after 2 hours
items.cause: Lamb neck is a slow-cooking cut; it can need more time.
items.fix: Re-cover and cook for a further 30 minutes. The meat should pull away from the bone with almost no pressure.

items.symptom: The bottom of the hotpot is dry and the lamb has caught
items.cause: Too little stock, or the casserole had gaps that let steam escape.
items.fix: Check the stock level after the first hour and top up with hot water or stock if needed. The casserole should be at least half-full of liquid throughout.

items.symptom: The potato slices have fallen apart
items.cause: A floury variety was used, which breaks down in a long braise.
items.fix: Use a waxy or all-rounder potato (Maris Piper or Desiree) that holds its shape. The slices will soften but should remain distinct.

content.text: Lancashire hotpot is one of the canonical dishes of northern English cooking, associated with the mill towns and farming country of Lancashire where lamb and potatoes were the staple ingredients. Early versions included oysters as a flavour base, but these were replaced by the end of the nineteenth century as the price of shellfish rose. The dish is the subject of a famous fictional dispute in William Makepeace Thackeray's writing and appears in the opening of Coronation Street. It is still made in the same form today.
